SOURCE: FireAct: Toward Language Agent Fine-tuning. Baian Chen*, Chang Shu*, Ehsan Shareghi, Nigel Collier, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao. arXiv:2310.05915v1 (9 Oct 2023), preprint (cs.CL).

COVERAGE: All 28 pages, 94,639 chars, extracted cleanly. Main text, all appendix results (A.1-A.9, B), and the references were read. The prompt appendix C (about pp. 22-28, few-shot IO/CoT/ReAct prompts) was only skimmed; it is prompt text.

Note: this is supervised fine-tuning (distillation) on filtered GPT-4 trajectories. There is no RL, reward optimisation or preference learning. "Reward = 1" only marks which trajectories to keep. Rejection-sampling SFT is the closest match to an RL-for-agents note.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Fine-tuning on GPT-4 ReAct trajectories improves HotpotQA EM over few-shot ReAct prompting for every base model; weaker models gain most.
  number: Llama-2-7B 14.8 to 26.2 (+77%); Llama-2-13B 21.2 to 34.4 (+62%); CodeLlama-7B +60%; CodeLlama-13B +39%; CodeLlama-34B +25%; GPT-3.5 31.4 to 39.2 (+25%)
  setup: 500 successful GPT-4 ReAct trajectories on HotpotQA, evaluated on 500 dev questions, Google search tool (SerpAPI), LoRA for open models. Standard errors are about 1.6-2.2 EM (Table 7), so some of the smaller gaps are within about 2 SE.
  quote: "Llama-2-7B 14.8 26.2 +11.4 / 77%" and "GPT-3.5 31.4 39.2 +7.8 / 25%"
  where: Table 2, p.5 (SEs in Table 7, p.17)
- A fine-tuned small open model can beat prompted stronger models, but not GPT-4.
  number: fine-tuned Llama-2-13B (34.4) beats all GPT-3.5 prompting (IO 22.4, CoT 28.0, ReAct 31.4). Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 (39.2) beats GPT-4 IO (37.2) but trails GPT-4 CoT (45.0) and ReAct (42.0).
  quote: "fine-tuned Llama-2-13B could outperform all GPT-3.5 prompting methods"; "could outperform GPT-4 + IO prompting but still lags behind GPT-4 + CoT/ ReAct prompting"
  where: Sec 5.1, p.5 (Table 1)
- Fine-tuning cuts inference cost and latency because few-shot examples are no longer needed in context.
  number: time 9.0s to 2.7s per trial (about 70%); cost 2.6e-3 to 2.2e-3 dollars, even with fine-tuned inference charged 8x per token
  setup: GPT-3.5, fine-tuned vs few-shot ReAct, HotpotQA. The authors say costs vary with conditions such as parallelism.
  quote: "the inference time is reduced by 70% (9.0s to 2.7s per trial), and the inference cost is reduced even though fine-tuned inference is charged 8× expensive"
  where: Sec 5.1, p.5 (Table 3, p.6)
  Note: the intro says "4x"; the 70% figure is about 3.3x.
- Fine-tuned agents are more robust to a noisy tool.
  number: with the search tool returning "None" half the time, EM goes FireAct 39.2 to 33.6 vs ReAct 31.4 to 20.8. With a random earlier response half the time, FireAct 37.2 vs ReAct 22.6.
  setup: GPT-3.5, HotpotQA, probability 0.5 of tool corruption. The paper's own text says the relative drops are 14.2% vs 33.8% ("None") and 5.1% vs 28.0% (random).
  quote: "lowered ReAct EM by 33.8% and FireAct EM only by 14.2%"; "random observations hurt ReAct by a similar degree (28.0% drop), but does not hurt FireAct much (only 5.1% drop)"
  where: Sec 5.2, p.6 (Table 3)
  Note: the authors' explanation, that the training trajectories contain noisy searches and GPT-4's successful reactions, is "possibly" and is not tested.
- Mixing methods in the data (CoT and Reflexion trajectories reformatted as ReAct) helps, and the best mix depends on the base model.
  number: GPT-3.5 HotpotQA EM: ReAct 39.4, ReAct+CoT 41.0, ReAct+Reflexion 38.8, ReAct+CoT+Reflexion 40.0. Intro: ReAct-only 39.2 (+25%) and ReAct+CoT 41.0 (+31%) vs prompted 31.4.
  setup: 500 ReAct + 187 CoT (reformatted as 1-round ReAct) + 47 long Reflexion trajectories (reflection prompted at the 6th and 10th round), all from GPT-4. Single seed; SE about 2.2.
  quote: "ReAct+CoT outperforms ReAct for GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 models, but hurts for CodeLlama models. ReAct+CoT+Reflexion is the worst for CodeLlama-7/13B, but is the best for CodeLlama-34B."
  where: Sec 6, p.7-8 (Table 4, Fig 4)
- Method selection at inference matters, and there is a large gap to an oracle.
  number: random method choice 32.4 EM; oracle (best method per question) 52.0
  quote: "The result of 32.4 is much lower than all multi-method agents ... But applying the best method for each instance leads to an “oracle” result of 52.0"
  where: Sec 6, p.8 (Table 4; Table 10, p.18)
- Multi-task data (HotpotQA, StrategyQA, MMLU) does not hurt the original task, and adding CoT data raises all four tasks.
  number: GPT-3.5 EM. HotpotQA-only: HotpotQA 39.2, Bamboogle 44.0. Multi-task: 39.2 / StrategyQA 55.5 / Bamboogle 43.2 / MMLU 63.2. Multi-task + CoT: 39.6 / 72.9 / 50.4 / 65.8.
  setup: successful GPT-4 ReAct and CoT trajectories. HotpotQA 500 ReAct + 277 CoT, StrategyQA 388 + 380, MMLU 456 + 469.
  quote: "Multi-task 39.2 55.5 43.2 63.2" and "+ CoT 39.6 72.9 50.4 65.8"
  where: Sec 7, p.8 (Table 5)
  Caveat: all fine-tuned agents underperform plain IO prompting on MMLU (68.6). Single-task HotpotQA fine-tuning does not transfer to StrategyQA or MMLU (not evaluated in the main table; see Table 14).
- Generalisation to a new task: a HotpotQA-tuned GPT-3.5 beats prompted GPT-3.5 on Bamboogle.
  number: 44.0 vs 40.8 EM
  setup: Bamboogle, 125 multi-hop questions (SE about 2.2, so the gap is small)
  quote: "the former (44.0 EM) still beats the latter (40.8 EM)"
  where: Sec 5.2, p.6
- Data scaling: GPT-3.5 is sample-efficient, while Llama models need more data to learn the format.
  number: GPT-3.5 reaches EM about 35 with 100 samples; Llama models cannot learn the ReAct format at 100 or 200 samples, and non-trivial scores "emerge" at 500; n in {100, 200, 500, 1000}. Llama-2-13B on 1,000 samples matches GPT-3.5 on 100.
  quote: "Llama models cannot even learn the ReAct format using 100 or 200 samples, but non-trivial scores “emerge” with 500 samples"
  where: Sec 5.3, p.6-7 (Fig 3)
- LoRA vs full fine-tuning (Llama-2-7B, 500 HotpotQA trajectories): full fine-tuning is better, but needs much more hardware.
  number: 30.2 vs 26.2 EM (+15.3%); LoRA 5.4 examples/s on one RTX 4090 vs 19.7 examples/s with full fine-tuning on 4 A100-80GB; adapter 38MB vs 14GB
  quote: "full-model fine-tuning (30.2 EM) outperforms LoRA fine-tuning (26.2 EM) by 15.3%"
  where: Sec 5.3 p.6; Table 11, Table 15 (pp.19, 21)
- Base-model effects are not monotonic. Coding specialisation helps at 7B but not 13B, and 34B is not always better.
  number: CodeLlama-7B 27.8 vs Llama-2-7B 26.2; CodeLlama-13B 29.0 vs Llama-2-13B 34.4; CodeLlama-34B 27.8 under ReAct-only data
  quote: "CodeLlama-7B outperforms Llama-2-7B, while CodeLlama-13B does not perform as well as Llama-2-13B"
  where: Sec 5.3, p.7 (Table 2)
- Appendix single-method, multi-task and multi-method runs under noisy tools:
  number: Table 9 (Normal / None / Random EM): single-task single-method 39.2/33.6/37.2; multi-task single-method 39.2/34.8/36.2; single-task multi-method 41.0/36.4/38.4; multi-task multi-method 39.6/35.2/37.0. Table 10 mixes range from 38.8 to 41.2.
  quote: "Single Task, Multi-method 41.0 36.4 38.4"
  where: p.18
- Masking observation tokens in the loss ("world modelling") has no consistent effect.
  number: e.g. CodeLlama-13B ReAct+CoT 24.8 masked vs 30.2 unmasked; CodeLlama-7B ReAct+CoT 24.0 vs 22.2
  quote: "learning world modelling does not have a consistent effect on performance"
  where: A.7, Table 13, p.19. Table 13's caption says Llama-2 but the rows are CodeLlama; the table is labelled inconsistently.
- Epochs: GPT-3.5 EM and F1 rise from 1 to 4 epochs, then F1 plateaus or dips.
  quote: "beyond 4 epochs, while EM scores continue to increase slightly, F1 scores plateau and even dip at times"
  where: A.8, Fig 7, pp.19-20
- Cost of a GPT-3.5 fine-tune: "around $10 per fine-tuning experiment in our case".
  where: Sec 8, p.9
- Discussion claim (a framing, not a result): prompting suits exploration, fine-tuning suits exploitation.
  quote: "prompting and fine-tuning seem more suitable for exploration and exploitation usecases respectively"
  where: p.9

METHOD DETAILS (for the note)
- Pipeline: GPT-4 few-shot generates trajectories on training questions. Only successful trajectories are kept (the Figure 2 caption says "successful trajectories are then converted into the ReAct format"; the appendix mentions "human-in-the-loop validation"). The result is distilled into a smaller LM, and few-shot prompts are not needed at inference. This is rejection-sampling SFT, not RL.
- The unified format is ReAct (thought / action / observation). A CoT trajectory becomes a single thought plus a finish action. Reflexion adds a reflection at rounds 6 and 10.
- Hyperparameters: GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 fine-tuned for 3 epochs through the OpenAI API. Llama and CodeLlama trained with LoRA (int8) for 30 epochs, lr 3e-4, batch 16. Step limit 11. Eval temperature 0.6 for open models, 0 for GPT-3.5. Dev subset of 500 from the 7,405 dev set; 2,000 train questions used for data curation.
- Tool: SerpAPI Google search returning the first of answer box, snippet, highlight words, or first result snippet.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "constrained to a single type of task (QA) and a single tool (Google search)". Only single-autoregressive-context methods are covered; multi-prompt, multi-role or multi-agent agents are unexplored. Multi-task covers only three QA tasks. The best fine-tunable LM is GPT-3.5.
- Open questions the authors leave: when to use tools or reflect (calibration), the best mix ratio of methods, and the gap to the 52.0 oracle.
- Not shown: no RL or online learning; no comparison against RL or preference methods; no seeds or confidence intervals beyond per-question standard errors; no ablation on trajectory-count vs diversity at fixed size (the diversity mixes also add more samples, so data quantity is confounded with diversity); teacher is GPT-4 (distillation ceiling, with fine-tuned GPT-3.5 still below GPT-4 CoT/ReAct).
- Has dated: 2023 models (GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613, Llama-2, CodeLlama) and a prompted GPT-4 baseline from mid-2023. Results were measured on open-domain QA with live Google search, which can drift.

BUILDS ON
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022b), including its PaLM-62B fine-tune beating prompted PaLM-540B; CoT (Wei et al., 2022b); Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023); distillation (Hinton et al., 2015); LoRA (Hu et al., 2022); STaR-style self-taught reasoning (Zelikman et al., 2022) and Huang et al. 2022a (fine-tuned small LMs beating prompted larger LMs); WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021); Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023); Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023); ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023); Press et al. 2022 (Bamboogle, search tool); multi-task instruction tuning (Longpre et al., 2023); datasets HotpotQA, StrategyQA, MMLU.

CODE: none in the paper. Code, data and checkpoints are at https://fireact-agent.github.io. Trajectory format worth keeping (from Fig 5 and the prompts): "Thought: ... / Action: search[...] / Observation: ... / Thought: I have the answer. / Action: finish[...]".

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p.3): FireAct pipeline. GPT-4 generates CoT/ReAct/Reflexion trajectories across tasks, incorrect ones are removed, the rest are reformatted as ReAct and used to fine-tune a smaller LM, and inference needs no few-shot prompt. The best single picture of the method.
- Fig 3 (p.6): data scaling curves, EM vs 100-1000 trajectories per model. Shows the emergence of the format at about 500.
- Fig 4 (p.6): EM per base LM per data mix (ReAct, +CoT, +Reflexion, both). Shows the non-monotonic effects.
- Fig 5 (p.7): qualitative trajectories. ReAct-only fine-tune gets distracted or loops; CoT+ReAct answers directly; Reflexion+ReAct pivots its search.
- Fig 6 (p.18): turn-count histograms per data mix; mixes shift the trajectory length distribution toward the training data's.
- Fig 1 (p.2): the intersection of agent and fine-tuning research (conceptual).

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean, apart from the figure text and some table column labels being jumbled. Table 8 loses its column headers; read it by position (HotpotQA, StrategyQA, Bamboogle, MMLU, as in Table 5).
- Table 10 and Table 4 disagree slightly on mix-method turn statistics. Table 10 has a four-method row of 39.4 EM with mu 2.4, and the ReAct+CoT+Reflexion row is 40.0 in Table 4 (sigma 4.8), so treat the two tables as separate runs or labelling.
- A.2 "Robustness analysis" heading has no body text.
- Section 5.3 and Table 7: "Table 7" is cited for the epochs figure, but it is Fig 7.
- A.4 says "ReAct+CoT (3.8 turns, 38.8 EM)", which should be ReAct+Reflexion.
- Multi-task rows: Table 9 "Multi-task, Multi-method 39.6" vs Table 5 "+ CoT 39.6" is consistent, but Table 9's multi-task single-method Normal EM is 39.2.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
